title: What happened to the other human species?

paragraphs.text: Nine human species walked the Earth 300,000 years ago. Now there is just one: modern humans – Homo sapiens. Included in these nine human species were Neanderthals, Homo neanderthalensis, who were stocky hunters well suited to Europe’s cold steppes. The related Denisovans inhabited Asia, while long-limbed Homo erectus lived in Indonesia, and Homo rhodesiensis in central Africa. Several short species survived alongside them: Homo naledi in South Africa, Homo luzonensis in the Philippines, Homo floresiensis in Indonesia, and the mysterious Red Deer Cave People in China. Given how quickly we’re discovering new species, more are likely waiting to be found.

By 10,000 years ago, all but one of these human species were gone. The disappearance of these species resembles a mass extinction. But there was no obvious environmental catastrophe – volcanic eruption, climate change, asteroid impact – that drove it. What is noteworthy, however, is that the timing of these extinctions suggests they were caused by the spread of Homo sapiens, who evolved 260,000-350,000 years ago in southern Africa.

The spread of modern humans out of Africa has led to other mass extinctions, extending from the disappearance of Ice Age mammals to the elimination of rainforests by civilisation today. But were other humans the first casualties? We are a uniquely dangerous species. We hunted woolly mammoths, ground sloths and moas to extinction. We eradicated plains and forests for farming, modifying over half the planet’s land area. We have altered the planet’s climate. But it is the fact that we compete for resources that makes us a danger to each other.

History is full of examples of people warring, displacing and wiping out other groups over territory, from Rome’s destruction of Carthage, to the American conquest of the West and the British colonisation of Australia. Like language or tool use, a capacity for and tendency to engage in genocide is arguably an intrinsic, instinctive part of human nature. There’s little reason to think that early Homo sapiens were less territorial, less violent or less intolerant.

Optimists have depicted early Homo sapiens as peaceful, noble savages, and have argued that our culture, not our nature, creates violence. But field studies, historical accounts, and archaeology all show that war in primitive cultures was intense, pervasive and lethal. Ancient weapons such as clubs, spears, axes and bows, combined with guerrilla tactics like raids and ambushes, were devastatingly effective.

It’s unlikely that other human species were much more peaceful. The existence of cooperative violence in male chimps suggests that war predates the evolution of humans, and Neanderthal skeletons show patterns of trauma consistent with warfare. The only difference is that sophisticated weapons likely gave Homo sapiens a military advantage over other human species. The arsenal of early Homo sapiens probably included projectile weapons like javelins and spears, as well as sticks and clubs.

Complex tools and culture would also have helped us efficiently harvest a wider range of animals and plants, feeding larger tribes, and giving our species a strategic advantage in numbers. But cave paintings, carvings and musical instruments hint at something far more dangerous: a sophisticated capacity for abstract thought and communication. The ability to cooperate, plan, strategise, manipulate and deceive may have been our ultimate weapon.

The incompleteness of the fossil record makes it hard to test these ideas. But in Europe, the only place with a relatively complete archaeological record, fossils show that within a few thousand years of our arrival, Neanderthals vanished. Traces of Neanderthal DNA in some Eurasian people prove we didn’t just replace them after they went extinct. Modern humans and Neanderthals met and interbred. Elsewhere, DNA tells of other encounters with archaic humans: East Asian, Polynesian and Australian groups have DNA from Denisovans; DNA from another species, possibly Homo erectus, occurs in many Asian people; African genomes show traces of DNA from yet another archaic species. The fact that we interbred with these other species proves that they disappeared only after encountering us.

But why would our ancestors wipe out their relatives, causing a mass extinction – or, perhaps more accurately, a mass genocide? The answer lies in population growth. Unchecked, we historically doubled our numbers every 25 years. And once Homo sapiens became cooperative hunters, working in packs, we were the top of the food chain – we hunted animals, but nothing hunted us. Without this control on our numbers, populations grew to exploit the available resources.

Further growth, or food shortages caused by prolonged lack of rainfall, harsh winters or overharvesting resources would inevitably lead tribes into conflict over food and foraging territory. Warfare became a check on population growth, perhaps the most important one. Our elimination of other species probably wasn’t a planned, coordinated effort of the sort practised by civilisations in more recent history, but a war of attrition. The end result, however, was just as final. Raid by raid, ambush by ambush, valley by valley, modern humans would have worn down their enemies.

Yet the extinction of Neanderthals, at least, took a long time – thousands of years. This was partly because early Homo sapiens lacked the advantages of later conquering civilisations: large numbers, supported by agriculture, and the devastation of their opponents due to contagious epidemics like smallpox, flu and measles. But while Neanderthals lost the war, to hold on so long they must have fought and won many battles against us, suggesting a level of intelligence close to our own.

Today, we look up at the stars and wonder if we’re alone in the universe. In fantasy and science fiction, we wonder what it might be like to meet other intelligent species, like us, but not us. It’s profoundly sad to think that we once did, and now they’re gone.
